9.category_hmdm_description: Among the molecules directly targeting viruses, nucleoside analogues form an essential class of broad-spectrum antiviral drugs. Unlike non-nucleoside polymerase inhibitors that often bind to allosteric non-conserved and mutation-tolerant sites, nucleoside analogues directly bind to the more conserved active site of the viral polymerase after conversion to their triphosphate active form. Nucleoside analogs represent the largest class of small molecule-based antivirals, which currently form the backbone of chemotherapy of chronic infections caused by HIV, hepatitis B or C viruses, and herpes viruses.

73.category_hmdm_description: Thymidine phosphorylase (TP) enzyme catalyzes the phosphorolysis of the nucleosides thymidine (dThd) and deoxyuridine (dUrd) to the corresponding bases thymine and uracil, and deoxyribose-1-phosphate. In lower organisms (e.g. Bacillus stearothermophilus) PYNP accepts both thymidine and uridine, whereas in mammalian and other higher organisms it is specific for thymidine (designated thymidine phosphorylase, TP). PYNP shares 40% sequence similarity (and presumably significant structural similarity) with human TP.

The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies some ANDs as human carcinogens.

295.category_hmdm_description: Glycoside hydrolases (GHs) (EC 3.2.1.X) hydrolyze glycosidic bonds between carbohydrates or between carbohydrate and non-carbohydrate components, for instance alcohols or phenols. To date, enzyme classification is based on amino acid similarities rather than substrate specificity. GHs are assigned to different groups based on conserved domains, and the families are numbered from 1 to 131 that are listed in the Carbohydrate-Active Enzymes Database. Glycoside hydrolases classified as GH2 were described to function as beta-galactosidase (EC 3.2.1.23) ; beta-mannosidase (EC 3.2.1.25); beta-glucuronidase (EC 3.2.1.31); alpha-L-arabinofuranosidase (EC 3.2.1.55); mannosylglycoprotein endo-beta-mannosidase (EC 3.2.1.152); exo-beta-glucosaminidase (EC 3.2.1.165); alpha-L-arabinopyranosidase (EC 3.2.1.-); beta-galacturonidase (EC 3.2.1.-); beta-xylosidase (EC 3.2.1.37); beta-D-galactofuranosidase (EC 3.2.1.146); beta-glucosidase (EC 3.2.1.21); beta-galacturonidase RGII specific (EC 3.2.1.-); glycyrrhizin beta-glucuronidase (EC 3.2.1.128). These enzymes hydrolyze their substrates through a retaining acid/base mechanism with two glutamic acid/glutamate residues involved. One residue acts as acid and base catalyst, whereas the other residue serves as nucleophile.

182.category_hmdm_description: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is characterized by prodromal symptoms, motor difficulties, and psychological or cognitive problems. 622.category_hmdm_description: Catechol O-methyltransferase catalyzes the methylation reaction whereby a methyl group from the cofactor S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) is transferred to one of the catecholic hydroxyls. Membrane-bound form COMT (MB-COMT) may be more relevant in inactivation of catecholaminergic neurotransmitters, whereas the soluble form (S-COMT) plays a more important role in inactivation of endogenous and xenobiotic catechols in other tissues. COMT is the primary enzyme that inactivates the catechol neurotransmitter dopamine and the drug L-dopa. L-dopa is used in the clinical treatment of central nervous system (CNS) disorders such as Parkinson's disease and possibly others (e.g. schizophrenia and depression). Its efficacy is associated with the level of dopamine converted from the drug. Studies have shown that inhibition of COMT activity results in marked reduction of the body clearance of L-dopa and dopamine, leading to a sustained level of dopamine in the brain and improved efficacy. The important role of COMT in treatment of Parkinson's disease has promoted an area wherein the aims are to design potent and selective COMT inhibitors. Several of these inhibitors have been used as adjuncts to L-dopa therapy.

302.category_hmdm_description: Escherichia coli thioesterase I (TAP) is a versatile enzyme possessing activities of thioesterase, esterase, arylesterase, protease, and lysophospholipase. E. coli thioesterase I, first identified by Barnes & Wakil, was cloned in 1993 and shown to catalyze hydrolytic cleavage of acyl-CoA thioesters. At the same time, protease I, named for its hydrolytic activity toward N-acetyl-dl-phenylalanine-2-naphthyl ester, was also cloned and characterized. Lysophospholipase L1, which catalyzes the hydrolysis of 1-acyl group of lysophospholipid was purified and its DNA sequence deduced in 1999. Recent studies showed that the gene sequences of E. coli thioesterase I (tesA), protease I (apeA) and lysophospholipase L1 (pldC) were identical and located at the same genomic position. Also, substrate competition assays showed that thioesterase I and protease I utilize the same active site, and all of them were identified as periplasmic proteins. The most plausible physiological role of TAP is that of lysophospholipase L1, since TAP shows specificity towards lysophospholipids and its activity on 1-acyl lysophosphatidylcholine follows typical Michaelis–Menten kinetics. TAP has stereoselectivity for amino acid derivative substrates, hence it is useful for the kinetic resolution of racemic mixtures of industrial chemicals.

622.category_hmdm_description: Catechol O-methyltransferase catalyzes the methylation reaction whereby a methyl group from the cofactor S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) is transferred to one of the catecholic hydroxyls. 619.category_hmdm_description: Pyridoxal 5′-phosphate (PLP) is a cofactor for about 4% of all biochemical reactions. PLP and five other ‘vitamers’, are collectively known as vitamin B6. In general, there are two independent de novo pathways that generate PLP: the deoxyxylulose 5′-phosphate (DXP)-dependent pathway, which is present in most eubacteria (e.g. Escherichia coli), and the ‘DXP-independent’ route, which is widespread (e.g. some eubacteria, Archaea, fungi and plants) and consists of a single enzyme complex, PLP synthase. In the PLP salvage pathway, however, different vitamers are interconverted using various kinase, phosphatase and pyridoxine/pyridoxamine 5′-phosphate oxidase (PNPOx) enzymes. The reaction catalysed by members of the PNPOx family (so-called PdxH proteins) is equivalent to the last step of the DXP-dependent PLP biosynthesis pathway, oxidizing either PNP or PMP to produce PLP. Members of the family utilize flavin mononucleotide (FMN) as a prosthetic group, oxidizing the C4′ alcohol (PNP) or amine (PMP) group to an aldehyde (PLP). During catalysis, FMN is used as the immediate electron acceptor and molecular oxygen as the final electron acceptor, forming hydrogen peroxide under aerobic conditions. Pyridoxal 5′-phosphate biosynthesis is essential for the survival and virulence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the organism that causes tuberculosis (TB) and is, for this reason, an important drug target at a time when resistance is rising and new drugs are urgently needed.

616.category_hmdm_description: Phospholipid N-methyltransferase (PLMT) enzymes catalyze the S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methylation of ethanolamine-containing phospholipids to produce phosphatidylcholine. In mammals and fungi, phosphatidylcholine can be formed through two distinct pathways: (a) the “nucleotide pathway” in which free choline is incorporated in phosphatidylcholine using CDP-choline as an intermediate, and (b) the “methylation pathway” whereby phosphatidylcholine is produced directly from phosphatidylethanolamine (PtdEtn) via three sequential methylation reactions using S-adenosylmethionine (AdoMet) as the methyl donor. In plants, phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis occurs through a branched pathway that utilizes components of both the nucleotide and methylation pathways. In mammals, the 18-kDa integral membrane protein phosphatidylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PEMT) is a PLMT that is expressed primarily in the liver. PEMT catalyzes all three of the methylation reactions needed to convert PtdEtn to phosphatidylcholine.

182.category_hmdm_description: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is characterized by prodromal symptoms, motor difficulties, and psychological or cognitive problems. 622.category_hmdm_description: Catechol O-methyltransferase catalyzes the methylation reaction whereby a methyl group from the cofactor S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) is transferred to one of the catecholic hydroxyls. Membrane-bound form COMT (MB-COMT) may be more relevant in inactivation of catecholaminergic neurotransmitters, whereas the soluble form (S-COMT) plays a more important role in inactivation of endogenous and xenobiotic catechols in other tissues. COMT is the primary enzyme that inactivates the catechol neurotransmitter dopamine and the drug L-dopa. L-dopa is used in the clinical treatment of central nervous system (CNS) disorders such as Parkinson's disease and possibly others (e.g. schizophrenia and depression). Its efficacy is associated with the level of dopamine converted from the drug. Studies have shown that inhibition of COMT activity results in marked reduction of the body clearance of L-dopa and dopamine, leading to a sustained level of dopamine in the brain and improved efficacy. The important role of COMT in treatment of Parkinson's disease has promoted an area wherein the aims are to design potent and selective COMT inhibitors. Several of these inhibitors have been used as adjuncts to L-dopa therapy.

616.category_hmdm_description: Phospholipid N-methyltransferase (PLMT) enzymes catalyze the S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methylation of ethanolamine-containing phospholipids to produce phosphatidylcholine. Phosphatidylcholine is the most abundant phospholipid in most non-plastid membranes of eukaryotes and functions as a structural membrane lipid, and as a precursor to important lipid-based signaling molecules. In mammals and fungi, phosphatidylcholine can be formed through two distinct pathways: (a) the “nucleotide pathway” in which free choline is incorporated in phosphatidylcholine using CDP-choline as an intermediate, and (b) the “methylation pathway” whereby phosphatidylcholine is produced directly from phosphatidylethanolamine (PtdEtn) via three sequential methylation reactions using S-adenosylmethionine (AdoMet) as the methyl donor. In plants, phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis occurs through a branched pathway that utilizes components of both the nucleotide and methylation pathways. In mammals, the 18-kDa integral membrane protein phosphatidylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PEMT) is a PLMT that is expressed primarily in the liver. PEMT catalyzes all three of the methylation reactions needed to convert PtdEtn to phosphatidylcholine.

505.category_hmdm_description: The core of each enzyme is similar: an alpha/beta sheet, not barrel, of eight beta-sheets connected by alpha-helices. These enzymes have diverged from a common ancestor so as to preserve the arrangement of the catalytic residues, not the binding site. They all have a catalytic triad, the elements of which are borne on loops which are the best-conserved structural features in the fold. The alpha/beta-hydrolase fold enzymes are one of the largest known protein families, including lipases, esterases, amidases, epoxide hydrolases, dehalogenases and hydroxynitrile lyases. The alpha/beta-hydrolase fold consists of eight beta-strands connected by alpha-helixes. These fold into a mostly parallel central beta-sheet surrounded by alpha-helixes. The catalytic triad consists of a nucleophile (serine, aspartate or cysteine), a histidine and a catalytic acid (aspartate or glutamate). These residues occur on conserved locations in loops and the alpha/beta-hydrolase fold brings them together to form the active site. Many alpha/beta-hydrolase fold enzymes also contain cap domains, the structures of which vary considerably between the different members. A cap domain sits on top of the active site, which is in the alpha/beta-hydrolase domain. In spite of their similar three-dimensional structures and similar active site residues, alpha/beta-hydrolase fold enzymes catalyse reactions with substrates containing a broad variety of functional groups, including carboxylic acid derivatives (esters, amides and thioesters), epoxides, alkyl halides and hydroxynitriles. The common mechanistic feature of these reactions is a nucleophilic attack.

300.category_hmdm_description: Non-proton pumping type II NADH dehydrogenase (NDH-2) plays a central role in the respiratory metabolism of bacteria, and in the mitochondria of fungi, plants and protists. The lack of NDH-2 in mammalian mitochondria and its essentiality in important bacterial pathogens suggests these enzymes may represent a potential new drug target to combat microbial pathogens. NADH dehydrogenases ensures adequate oxidation of NADH to NAD+. Most species possess one to two isozymes of the non-proton-translocating type 2 dehydrogenase (Ndh), also termed alternative NADH dehydrogenase. While complex I is deeply integrated into the inner membrane, alternative NADH dehydrogenases are not membrane-embedded, but rather associated to the membrane surface, either on the IMS side (external NADH dehydrogenases) or the matrix side (internal NADH dehydrogenases). Unlike complex I, alternative NADH dehydrogenase lack flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and iron-sulfur clusters as reactive groups. Instead, they contain a flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) cofactor to mediate the electron transfer from NAD(P)H to ubiquinone. Alternative NADH dehydrogenase can serve as important valves on the respiratory chain when oxygen tensions suddenly rise. NADH dehydrogenases also serve as as ‘apoptosis inducing factors’ in a poorly understood process that involves the formation of a toxic protein fragment on the outside or inside of the mitochondrial outer membrane and in animals but not in yeast, AIFM1 serves as biogenesis factor for MIA40 and thus, indirectly, for many IMS proteins.

DHDR is involved in the reduction of (S)- and (R)-dihydrodaidzein, (S)- and (R)-DHD,  to trans- and cis-tetrahydrodaidzein (trans- and cis-THD), respectively.

These enzymes hydrolyze their substrates through a retaining acid/base mechanism with two glutamic acid/glutamate residues involved. One residue acts as acid and base catalyst, whereas the other residue serves as nucleophile.

606.category_hmdm_description: The pfkB family of enzymes across kingdoms includes ribokinases, phosphofructokinases, adenosine kinases (ADKs) and several others with diverse substrate specificities. Typical PfkB protein structure is a large domain consisting of a beta-sheet sandwiched between several alpha-helices, and a smaller domain, known as the lid domain, comprised of another beta-sheet attached to the larger domain by short loops that act as a hinge. Binding of substrates to pfkB proteins follows ordered bi-bi kinetics where the carbohydrate enters first, followed by ATP. PfkB proteins possess two signature motifs: a di-gly (GG) motif in the N-terminal region and a G/AXGD motif in the C-terminal region. The role of each motif has been identified through mutational and structural analyses. The GG motif provides flexibility in the hinge region that connects the lid and the large domain. The aspartate in the G/AXGD motif acts as a base during catalysis and activates the C6 fructose hydroxyl group for nucleophilic attack on the gamma-phosphate in ATP. Many pfkB proteins are active as dimers generated through interactions between the lid domains of two monomers. Aside from their regulation by ATP, pfkB family enzymes are activated by both monovalent and divalent cationic cofactors.
